messages.subject: Watkins marine mammal sound database and seewave::acoustat()
messages.subject_clean: Watkins marine mammal sound database and seewave::acoustat()
messages.body_plain:
Hi

i am working on a little open source project[0], to make 15254 sound
clips from the Watkins marine mammal sound database more accessible and
useful for researchers.

One feature would be, to filter the sounds by signal characteristics and
properties.

The technical workflow, for effectively analyzing ~15.000 short sound
clips, is already in place and documented[1], however i am looking for
some advice on what R/seewave methods to use, given the wide variety of
signals in the database.

Current topics and question are:

- What noise reduction should be used?

- How to get comparable results, when sound clips vary in sample rate?
Is that an issue?

- How to distinguish marine mammals by sound characteristics?

- How to distinguish different vocalization types (whistles, clicks, etc)

I am looking for code examples as well as general ideas and advice on
how to proceed with the task. Any contributions to the project are welcomed.

Thank you
   D.Leucas

[0]: https://marine-mammal.soundwave.cl
[1]:
https://marine-mammal.soundwave.cl/changelog.html#july-2018-analyzing-watkins-sound-clips-for-acoustic-features

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jérémy,

It's hard to say what the maximum file size must be. It depends on the file and on your computer.

To analyze in sections, you could cut it into smaller waves (using the cutw() function or an external program).

Also consider down-sampling. To me, it looks like your file has a really high sampling rate. Depending on what you're trying to analyze, you might be able to get away with a lower sampling rate. To down-sample, take a look at the reamp() function and try something like this, where 'g' is the new sampling frequency.

wave_small <- resamp(wave, g = 44100, output = "Wave")

Once, again, though, the approach you take depends on what you're trying to do with the results. I'm not familiar with the th index, so I can't help you out much there.

Good luck!

Steffi
Dr. Stefanie LaZerte
Biologist, R and CitSci Enthusiast
http://steffilazerte.ca/

messages.subject: Re: [seewave] Compute acoustic dissimilarity index
messages.body_plain:
Dear Jérémy
The function diffspec() computes the dissimilarity index between two frequency spectra (denoted D[f] in the text below).
The function diffenv() computes the dissimilarity index between two amplitude envelope (denoted D[t] in the text below).
The function diffwave() computes the dissimilarity index as the product of of D[f] and D[t] (denoted D in the text below).

Note that there is also diffcumspec() to compute the dissimilarity index between two cumulatedfrequency spectra (denoted D[cf], see Lellouch et al 2014https://www.researchgate.net/publication/260680408_Monitoring_temporal_change_of_bird_communities_with_dissimilarity_acoustic_indices).

HTH

Jerome

messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

One explanation could be that a relatively flat response is interpreted as being close to the maximum possible diversity. If you have for example 30 animal species in a sample de diversity is maximum if each one has a frequincy of 1/30th. You could have 60 species in a sample but if their frequencies are very skewed (i.e., two or three species dominate) the overall diversity would be lower, like with a sudden bird call followed by background noise.

Hope this helps!

Juan
